The reason is a name, not a flow: New York Fed President Williams told Bloomberg on October 13 that one more hike this year may still be appropriate and that he sees no reason the Fed would need to do more after that, and the dollar fell against all seven majors on the session. update.title: 🇦🇺 AUD analysis updated
update.text: Employment -39.3K vs +19.6K forecast and unemployment 4.7% vs 4.6%, both TE-verified. AUD cut +2 to +1, the only major lower on a falling dollar. Oct 28 CPI now carries Nov 3.

dailyRead: Yesterday this report put the dollar at plus 2 and said the reason was the 2027 dot distribution - 8 of 18 participants at 4.375%, 14 of 18 at or above the 4.1% median - because that is a better argument than the 2026 dots everyone quotes. Overnight the New York Fed President, a permanent voter and one of those 18 dots, told Bloomberg he currently sees no need for a rate hike in 2027. Williams kept December alive, saying he has not changed his view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike and that at this time he has no reason to think the Fed would need to do more after that. That is not a dovish turn on December; it is a cap on everything past it, and it came from the single most important voice on the committee after the Chair. The market read it exactly that way: the dollar fell against all seven majors on Tuesday, the ten-year eased about 3bp to 5.2070, and DXY gave back Monday's 18-month high at roughly 102.60 to sit at 102.101. So the dollar comes down to plus 1 - the December leg is intact and still the best-supported hike on the board, but the leg this report named yesterday as the reason for plus 2 was publicly withdrawn by its own author. The second change is the euro, and it is larger than the price suggests. Lagarde spoke in Bangkok this morning on the sidelines of the IMF meetings and moved off the line this file has quoted for a week. She had been saying she saw no evidence at this stage of energy feeding into wages; today she said euro-area inflation is driven predominantly, but not exclusively, by higher energy prices linked to the Iran war, that the Council has not yet seen second-round effects but is watching early signals especially in wage negotiations, and then the sentence that matters - we cannot wait until they're there in full view, but we can anticipate. That is a central bank telling you it will move on the forecast rather than the outturn, with a December 17 meeting that 64 of 73 economists already expect to deliver. At the same time she put France's borrowing costs back on Paris, saying the primary and first solution lies at home in France and that it has to do with fiscal policies, without ruling out the Transmission Protection Instrument - and OAT-Bund narrowed to 137.52bp on TE's October 13 closes from the 142.98bp this report carried yesterday. Two of the euro's three legs improved in one morning, so the euro goes to plus 1 with the honest caveat that spot has confirmed almost nothing: EUR/USD at 1.12073 is plus 0.08% on the day and still the worst major year to date at minus 4.54%. Third, Canada. The leg that cut this currency to minus 2 and then restored it to minus 1 has now extended for a second consecutive session: WTI at 94.810 is plus 7.40% on the week and within 5.5% of the hundred dollars Macklem said in Halifax would push inflation up in the coming months rather than the temporary gasoline move the Bank can look through. USD/CAD has fallen two sessions to 1.41989. CAD goes to 0, and it is capped there rather than higher only by the labour market - minus 68.3K in September with unemployment at 6.5% is not a currency you buy on an oil headline. Macklem speaks at 06:05 UTC today and again Friday, and the October 28 Monetary Policy Report introduces the Bank's new Prima model. Fourth, the oil story itself has broadened and become genuinely two-sided for the first time in two weeks, which is why the two crude benchmarks split on Tuesday: Brent settled 105.69, down 96 cents, while WTI settled 94.14, up 40 cents. The bullish side is unchanged and still severe - Houthi strikes hit Riyadh's main airport, Trump said the US may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, a tanker and a container ship were struck in the Strait on Tuesday per UKMTO notices, and CENTCOM said US forces helped partners move more than 19 million barrels through on Monday, which is a number you only publish when transit is the problem. The bearish side is new: Trump said Russia would supply diesel to global markets and his administration temporarily eased sanctions on Russian fuel, Saudi Arabia said its exports are not at risk, and OPEC reported a sharp September production gain led by Saudi Arabia. Goldman's arithmetic is the useful check - an extra 800,000 tonnes of diesel is worth only one to two dollars a barrel wholesale, against US inventories down 14% year on year and visible Chinese stocks down 11% - so the relief is real but small against the risk. Keep USOIL long and note it is a rally inside a monthly downtrend, minus 10.41% on the month. Everything else is positioning into 12:30. Australia is the strongest currency on the board and the best major on the session, plus 0.27% and back above the 0.70 pivot at 0.70024, carrying Monday's minutes where members expressed concern that excess demand was greater than previously assessed; employment at 00:30 UTC tomorrow, forecast plus 19.6K against plus 39.5K, is the next test. Sterling holds plus 1 into four Bailey appearances this week and a GDP print tomorrow forecast at minus 0.1% m/m, which is the growth-side risk to a November 5 hike priced across a 75-90% range. The yen stays at 0 for the unglamorous reason that the differential went the wrong way: US ten-year 5.2070 against JGB 3.0010 is 220.60bp, wider than the 219.40bp carried yesterday, because JGBs rallied alongside Treasuries. The franc stays at 0 and failed its haven test again - EUR/CHF at 0.93229 is above yesterday's 0.93096 in a week of strikes on Riyadh and Hormuz. And gold is the cleanest illustration of the regime: 4165.35 is minus 3.58% year to date, in a year with a war, a disrupted Strait and crude up 65%, because the Fed spent that year hiking. Williams capping 2027 is the first crack in that, which is why gold is plus 1.32% on the week - but it has failed every war headline this month and stays RANGE until a soft core print turns it.

today.headline: Cut from +2 to +1. September employment fell 39.3K against a plus 19.6K forecast and unemployment rose to 4.7% against 4.6% expected - both of the invalidation triggers this file published yesterday - and AUD/USD at 0.69561 is the only major lower against a dollar that is itself down 0.34%.
today.read: This is the cleanest attribution on the board today, because the dollar leg removes itself from the argument: DXY is minus 0.34%, EUR/USD plus 0.35%, GBP/USD plus 0.32%, NZD/USD plus 0.31% and USD/JPY minus 0.32%, and AUD/USD is minus 0.23% at 0.69561. Seven majors, one of them lower, and it is the one that just printed its own data. Both lines are TE-verified on the Sep/26 rows - employment change minus 39.3K against a plus 19.6K forecast and plus 39.5K prior, unemployment 4.7% against 4.6% expected and 4.6% prior, which clears the level pre-release previews were already describing as a five-year high. Yesterday's entry named the trigger in advance: plus 2 was invalidated by a print materially below plus 19.6K or unemployment above 4.6%, and the release delivered both at once, so the downgrade to plus 1 is the file keeping its own word rather than a reaction to the headline. The composition is where the analysis actually sits, and it is far less dovish than minus 39.3K reads. TE's labour page carries full-time employment at plus 34,400 after minus 6,300 in August, part-time at minus 73,700 after plus 45,775, and the participation rate at 66.80% from 67.10%. That is an exact mirror of August, when a plus 39.5K headline concealed a 6,300 fall in full-time jobs - so across the two months net employment is roughly flat while the mix has rotated from part-time into full-time, which is the better of the two for income and demand. And participation fell three tenths: a shrinking labour force normally flatters the unemployment rate, so 4.7% was reached despite that, which is the genuinely soft part of the report. The policy read turns on a line in the September minutes that matters more today than it did yesterday. The Bank's own economists were recorded increasingly questioning whether the rate of unemployment consistent with the inflation target was higher than previously assessed - if the RBA thinks the NAIRU has risen, then 4.7% is less disinflationary than the print looks, and the same minutes show a committee prepared to accept slower growth and weaker employment to bring inflation down. The RBA pre-authorised this outturn, which is why the currency is cut one notch rather than two. Pre-release pricing had November at roughly 30 to 40 percent, with Nomura's Andrew Ticehurst at 40% from 30% and one report splitting hike odds across November 31%, December 25% and February 28%; those previews said plainly that a 4.7% unemployment rate would strengthen the case against November. No post-release pricing was published anywhere at the time of writing, so those stay labelled as pre-print marks rather than today's. The terms of trade stopped helping as well, which is the second change: copper at 6.5672 USD/lb is minus 0.67% on the day and its year-to-date gain has been trimmed to 15.58% from the 18.31% this file carried yesterday, while iron ore at 90.74 USD/T remains minus 15.30% on the year. November 3 is now a single-number event. Q3 CPI on October 28, six days before the meeting, with the trimmed mean at 3.6% for three straight months, carries the entire hawkish case; the labour market has stopped carrying any of it.

today.headline: Restored from +1 to +2. September CPI ran above forecast on three of four lines - core 0.3% m/m against a 0.2% consensus, core 2.6% y/y against 2.5%, headline 3.7% y/y against 3.6%, headline 0.6% m/m in line - and the dollar is bid against six of seven majors.
today.read: This is the hawkish side of the binary this report named at 05:23 UTC, and the file said in advance what it would do: core at 0.3% m/m restores the dollar to plus 2 and reopens October 28. All four lines are TE-verified on the Sep/26 rows - core CPI 0.3% m/m against a 0.2% consensus and level with the 0.3% prior, core 2.6% y/y against 2.5% and up from 2.4%, headline 3.7% y/y against 3.6% and up from 3.4%, and headline 0.6% m/m exactly in line. The in-line headline matters as much as the core beat: September's energy spike was fully anticipated, so the entire surprise came from the part that is not oil. TE's own detail says the same thing from both sides - energy inflation is 20.40% from 16.30%, which is the expected spike, while core accelerated underneath it and one-year consumer inflation expectations rose to 3.90% from 3.60%. A third consecutive 0.3% core month is the specific problem for a committee that has spent two meetings looking through a supply shock, because the three-month run annualises near 3.6% against the 2.4% core y/y the Fed cited in September. The price reaction was broad rather than concentrated, which is the signature of a rates repricing rather than a single-pair move: DXY went from 102.101 at minus 0.10% to 102.448 at plus 0.26%, EUR/USD fell to 1.11543 at minus 0.40%, USD/CHF rose 0.45% to 0.83634, USD/JPY cleared 158.50 to 158.681 at plus 0.22%, GBP/USD is minus 0.18% at 1.32307 and NZD/USD minus 0.22% at 0.55994. Only two currencies held: AUD/USD at 0.69891 is still plus 0.07% though it gave back the 70c pivot, and USD/CAD at 1.42098 is still minus 0.05% because WTI went through 95 to 95.363 in the same hour. The honest limit on this upgrade is that it does not restore the ceiling. Williams capped 2027 on Tuesday and a September core print cannot un-say it, so this is a stronger near leg on an unchanged far leg - plus 2 rather than the plus 3 a pre-Williams version of this print would have earned. Post-print probabilities are not yet verifiable: centralbank.watch still read 22.0% for an October 28 hike and 78.0% for a hold within ten minutes of the release, which is the pre-print number rather than a refreshed one. Chairman Warsh speaks as a red folder on Friday at 03:30 UTC with this number in hand and is the one voice that can reset both legs; September PPI and retail sales at 12:30 UTC tomorrow test whether the energy shock is passing through at the producer level.

today.headline: Raised from 0 to +1. Lagarde moved from seeing no evidence of energy feeding into wages to saying the Council can anticipate second-round effects rather than wait for them, and OAT-Bund narrowed to 137.52bp from 142.98bp.
today.read: Two of the euro's three legs improved in one morning and the better one is the policy leg, because it is a change in language rather than a change in a spread. Speaking at a CNN event in Bangkok on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings, Lagarde said euro-area inflation is driven predominantly, but not exclusively, by higher energy prices linked to the Iran war; that the Council has not yet seen second-round effects in broader prices but is watching early signals, especially in wage negotiations; and then the sentence to trade - we cannot wait until they're there in full view, but we can anticipate. For a week this file has quoted her saying she saw no evidence at this stage of energy prices feeding into wages, and that line was the single best argument against the December hike that 64 of 73 economists in the Reuters poll of October 5-8 already expect. It is now replaced by a statement that the Council will act on the forecast. With September HICP at 3.8%, nearly double target, and new staff projections landing exactly at the December 17 meeting, that is the shape of a bank that hikes. The second leg is France and she handled it hawkishly too, declining to take the problem onto the ECB's balance sheet: some countries face disproportionate borrowing costs, with France being a case in point, but the primary and first solution lies at home in France and it has to do with fiscal policies. She did not rule out the Transmission Protection Instrument. OAT-Bund narrowed to 137.52bp on TE's October 13 closes, the OAT at 4.8360% against the Bund at 3.4608%, from the 142.98bp carried here yesterday, and it narrowed through the opening days of the plenary debate on the 2027 budget rather than despite them. The third leg is unchanged and is the reason this is plus 1 and not more: the price has confirmed nothing. EUR/USD at 1.12073 is plus 0.08% on the day, plus 0.10% on the week, minus 2.91% on the month and still the worst major year to date at minus 4.54%. The political calendar also still has teeth - the solemn vote on the revenue half of the budget is October 20, the social security bill October 27 and the whole text November 17, with a censure motion possible at any point and the ordinance route shut until December 17 at midnight. Lagarde speaks again at 08:30 UTC today, the EU Economic Summit runs today and tomorrow, and the October 29 meeting is expected to hold by 70 of the same 73 economists.

today.headline: Raised from -1 to 0. WTI at 94.810 is plus 7.40% on the week and within 5.5% of the hundred dollars Macklem named as the level that would push inflation up, and USD/CAD has fallen two consecutive sessions to 1.41989.
today.read: This is the second upgrade in two days on the same leg, which needs justifying rather than repeating. The leg has extended materially rather than oscillated: WTI went 90.409, then 92.715, then 94.810 across three readings of this file, plus 7.40% on the week with Brent plus 6.13%, and it is now inside 5.5% of a threshold the Governor named himself. In Halifax on September 21 Macklem said that if oil prices stay near US$100 a barrel the Bank would expect inflation to edge up in the coming months, that it has been looking through the direct impact of higher oil so far but the risk of it becoming more persistent has increased, and separately that there is a risk in delaying a hike too long. He also called the Middle East war a bigger inflation issue than US tariffs. Against that, the Bank's own published baseline assumes crude falls toward 75 dollars by mid-2027, so the assumption is now wrong by roughly 20 dollars rather than marginally. The currency has started to price it: USD/CAD at 1.41989 is minus 0.12% on the day and minus 0.40% on the week, a second consecutive session lower, though it is still plus 2.01% on the month and plus 3.49% year to date, so this is a turn rather than a trend. The reason this stops at 0 and does not go positive is the domestic side, and it is genuinely bad. September employment fell 68.3K with full-time down 35.4K, unemployment rose to 6.5%, the employment rate fell to 60.6% and wage growth slowed to 3.2% from 3.39%. Headline CPI is 3.0% with core at 2.4%, both of which a central bank can live with. That is not a labour market that tolerates a hike, which is why TD still expects a hold through 2026 even while markets price at least one move before year-end. Two dated risks: Macklem speaks at 06:05 UTC today and 04:15 UTC Friday, and October 28 brings a Monetary Policy Report produced on the Bank's new Prima model, where the crude assumption gets rewritten in public.

today.headline: Unchanged at +1 with the risk rotating from the inflation side to the growth side: GDP m/m tomorrow is forecast at minus 0.1% against plus 0.4%, and Bailey speaks four times this week.
today.read: The hawkish case is intact and unchanged. The committee split 6-3 on September 17 with three members voting for 25bp to 4.00%, Bank Rate is TE-verified at 3.75%, August CPI is 3.1% with core at 2.6%, and November 5 carries a Monetary Policy Report and is priced across a 75-90% range depending on source rather than as a near-certainty. The energy condition Bailey set himself keeps tightening: UK gas at 215.00 GBp/thm is plus 11.04% on the week and plus 191.29% year to date, against his formulation that higher energy costs have had a limited effect on wages and prices so far, but the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate. What changes today is where the risk sits. GDP m/m at 06:00 UTC tomorrow is forecast at minus 0.1% after plus 0.4%, and a contraction is the first clean argument the six who held in September would have for holding again - the UK is the only G10 economy on this board where the hike case has to be defended against the growth data rather than the inflation data. The labour market is already soft underneath the headline: payrolled employees fell 26.1K, wage growth slowed to 3.9% from 4.2%, and the 4.9% unemployment rate has been flat for three readings while the employment change of plus 67K came in below the prior 83K. Sterling at 1.32734 is plus 0.14% on the day and plus 0.45% on the week, the second-best major today, but still minus 1.38% year to date. Bailey spoke at 05:30 UTC this morning, speaks again at 07:30 UTC tomorrow, as a red folder at 02:00 UTC Friday and at 06:45 UTC Saturday - four chances to move the 75-90% range in either direction.

today.headline: Unchanged at 0 for an arithmetic reason rather than a policy one: the ten-year gap widened to 220.60bp from 219.40bp because JGBs rallied alongside Treasuries when Williams capped the US terminal rate.
today.read: The forward pricing is the firmest the yen has carried in this file and it still is not enough. Swaps imply roughly 90% for a BoJ hike by December; the October 29-30 meeting, confirmed from boj.or.jp, is settled as a hold at 91-94% across prediction markets and 91% on centralbank.watch as of October 9; and the Outlook Report lands October 30, which is where a path change would actually be published rather than at the December 17-18 meeting that carries no Outlook Report. The problem is that the yen is paid to wait and the waiting got no cheaper. The US ten-year at 5.2070% against the JGB at 3.0010% is 220.60bp, wider than the 219.40bp carried yesterday, because the Williams headline rallied both curves rather than just the Treasury curve. A Fed that still delivers in December while the BoJ is 90% to move in the same month leaves the expected differential roughly where it was, and the spot differential - the thing that actually funds the carry trade - widened. USD/JPY at 158.159 is minus 0.11% on the day and plus 0.05% on the week, back below the 158.50 area where intervention commentary starts; Japan is reported to have intervened in late July with US participation, and the finance ministry has said future dollar-selling intervention would be financed through the Fed's FIMA repo facility, which is an unusual arrangement and the reason the threat is not empty. The domestic data supports the hike without demanding it: CPI 1.9% with core at 1.7%, down from 1.8%, unemployment 2.5%, wage growth 3.8% after 4.3%, annual growth 0.7%. The structural case - a government that has stopped treating deflation as the binding constraint - remains the under-priced one, and October 30 is where it gets tested.

today.headline: Unchanged at -1 and the new evidence runs against it: ANZ says the Selected Price Indexes confirmed downside risk to its own and the RBNZ's Q3 CPI forecasts, which is the leg the hawkish tail was built on.
today.read: This is the weakest currency on the board and the single argument that kept it from minus 2 is now under pressure from the bank closest to the data. The hawkish tail here was always inflation: Q2 CPI printed 4.1% against 3.1% prior, Westpac has inflation finishing 2026 above 4%, and BNZ's outlier call for an October hike and an eventual 3.75% OCR rests entirely on that persistence. ANZ's commentary of October 9 says the Selected Price Indexes confirmed some downside risk to our and the RBNZ's Q3 CPI forecasts, and Q3 CPI is the final major domestic release before the decision. If that print lands soft the tail disappears and what is left is 5.6% unemployment, the highest on this board, a 2.75% official cash rate that is the second lowest, annual wage growth of 2.1%, and a negative differential to the dollar that no amount of a 2.6% growth rate compensates for. The October 28 meeting is a Monetary Policy Review rather than a full Statement, which limits how much the Bank can reframe anything, and centralbank.watch carries 88% for no change; Westpac expects the pause then 3.00% in December and TE's forecast rows agree at 2.75% then 3.00% on December 9. The currency is participating in today's dollar move but no more than that: NZD/USD at 0.56259 is plus 0.25% on the day and plus 0.46% on the week, against minus 2.28% on the month and minus 2.26% year to date, and the ten-year is 5.0050%. Keep the shorts in the crosses rather than against a dollar that just had its terminal rate capped - NZD is the short leg, not the dollar the long one.

today.headline: Unchanged at 0 and the haven test failed again: EUR/CHF rose to 0.93229 from 0.93096 in a week with strikes on Riyadh's main airport and two more vessels hit in the Strait.
today.read: The finding here is negative and it keeps replicating, which makes it useful. This week offered as clean a haven test as the calendar can produce - Houthi strikes on Riyadh's main airport, Trump saying the US may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, a tanker and a container ship struck in the Strait on Tuesday per UKMTO notices, the US Navy engaging Iranian-linked vessels - and the franc lost ground to both of its reference currencies. EUR/CHF at 0.93229 is above yesterday's 0.93096 and comfortably above the 0.93 Rabobank expects to hold; USD/CHF at 0.83186 is minus 0.09% on the day and minus 0.18% on the week but still plus 4.91% year to date for the dollar. A currency that cannot bid on that news flow is not a haven in this regime, and the reason is that the haven premium is being competed away by yield - the franc pays 0.00% while every other central bank on this board is hiking or has just hiked. That is the case for keeping the franc crosses at RANGE or short rather than reaching for a haven trade on the next headline, and for taking EUR/CHF long now that the ECB has turned pre-emptive. Policy offers nothing in either direction: the September statement dropped the appreciation bias, Martin hinted on October 8 at lower-for-long rather than a return to negative rates, and inflation at 1.0% in September with core at 0.5% and unemployment at 3.0% gives the Bank no reason to act before December 10. The dated items are Chairman Schlegel at 04:30 UTC tomorrow and the policy meeting minutes on October 22, and the live risk on both is intervention language rather than the rate.

That defends December 9, which Williams never questioned, and it reopens October 28 from a pre-print 22.0%. What the print does not do is restore the ceiling above December. Williams told Bloomberg on October 13 that he has not changed his view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike and that at this time he has no reason to think the Fed would need to do more after that, and a September core reading cannot un-say a statement about 2027, so the far leg stays disowned by one of its own dots. September was unanimous 12-0 with all 19 officials backing it in the October 7 minutes, and the projection medians still read 4.1% for 2026 and 2027, 3.9% for 2028 and 3.6% for 2029 against a 3.2% longer run, with PCE 3.7%, core PCE 3.4%, GDP 2.3% and unemployment 4.1%. Chairman Warsh speaks as a red folder on October 16 at 03:30 UTC - two days after this print, with the number in hand - and is the only voice that outranks the one that moved the market on Tuesday. September PPI and retail sales at 12:30 UTC tomorrow are the producer-level pass-through check.

EUR.when: October 29, where a Reuters poll of October 5-8 has 70 of 73 economists expecting no change; the hike is December 17, expected by 64 of 73 of the same panel, taking the deposit rate to 2.75%.
EUR.note: TE re-verified the deposit facility rate at 2.50% (main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%), raised from 2.25% in September. Lagarde changed the operative sentence this morning. Speaking at a CNN event in Bangkok on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings, she said euro-area inflation is driven predominantly, but not exclusively, by higher energy prices linked to the Iran war, that the Council has not yet seen second-round effects in broader prices but is watching early signals especially in wage negotiations, and then - we cannot wait until they're there in full view, but we can anticipate. Set that against the line this report has quoted for a week, that she saw no evidence at this stage of energy prices feeding into wages, and the posture has moved from waiting for evidence to acting on the forecast. With HICP at 3.8% in September, nearly double target, and new projections arriving on December 17, that is the configuration a December hike is made of. On France she declined to carry the fiscal problem, saying some countries face disproportionate borrowing costs with France being a case in point but that the primary and first solution lies at home in France and it has to do with fiscal policies; she did not rule out the Transmission Protection Instrument. OAT-Bund narrowed to 137.52bp on TE's October 13 closes, with the OAT at 4.8360% and the Bund at 3.4608%, from 142.98bp yesterday. She speaks again at 08:30 UTC today.

GBP.when: November 5 with a Monetary Policy Report, priced across a 75-90% range depending on source, with December 17 the following meeting.
GBP.note: TE re-verified Bank Rate at 3.75%, held since the 6-3 vote on September 17 at which the three dissenters wanted 25bp to 4.00%. The committee and the energy input remain the two live legs and neither changed overnight. Bailey's own formulation is the forward guidance that matters: higher energy costs have had a limited effect on wages and prices so far, but the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate. UK gas at 215.00 GBp/thm is plus 11.04% on the week and plus 191.29% year to date, so that condition keeps tightening. The new risk is on the other side of the mandate: GDP m/m at 06:00 UTC tomorrow is forecast at minus 0.1% against plus 0.4% prior, and a contraction is the first thing that would give the three holdouts on the committee a reason to stay put. Bailey speaks four times this week - 05:30 UTC today, 07:30 UTC tomorrow, a red folder at 02:00 UTC on Friday and 06:45 UTC on Saturday.

JPY.when: October 29-30, confirmed from boj.or.jp, with the Outlook Report released on October 30; December 17-18 is the following meeting and carries no Outlook Report.
JPY.note: TE re-verified the policy rate at 1.25% after the September 18 hike from 1.00%. October is settled - centralbank.watch had 91% for no change as of October 9 and prediction markets 91-94% - while swaps still imply roughly 90% for a hike by December, the firmest forward number the yen has carried in this file. The reason that does not lift the score is arithmetic rather than policy: the ten-year gap widened to 220.60bp, with the US at 5.2070% and the JGB at 3.0010%, against 219.40bp yesterday, because JGBs rallied alongside Treasuries when Williams capped the US terminal rate. The yen needs the gap to compress, and a Fed that still delivers December while the BoJ waits until the same month does not compress it. USD/JPY at 158.159 is minus 0.11% and back below the 158.50 level where intervention talk starts; Japan is reported to have intervened in late July with US participation, and the finance ministry has said future dollar-selling would be financed through the Fed's FIMA repo facility. The structural case is the Outlook Report on October 30, not the decision.

AUD.when: Still a hike rather than a hold or a cut, but November 3 is no longer the likely date after the September employment miss, and the weight shifts to December and February; Q3 CPI on October 28 now has to carry November on its own.
AUD.note: TE re-verified the cash rate at 4.60% after the unanimous September 29 hike from 4.35%. September employment is TE-verified at minus 39.3K against a plus 19.6K forecast with unemployment at 4.7% against 4.6% expected, and that is the first hard data point to contradict the September minutes, in which members expressed concern that excess demand was greater than previously assessed. Pre-release coverage of those minutes had November priced around 30 to 40 percent - Nomura's Andrew Ticehurst lifted his estimate to 40% from 30%, with one report splitting hike pricing roughly evenly across November at 31%, December at 25% and February at 28% - and the same previews said explicitly that an unemployment rate at 4.7% would strengthen the case against a November rise. Post-release pricing was not yet published anywhere when this ran, so treat those as the pre-print marks. Two things stop this becoming a dovish turn. The minutes record the Bank's own economists increasingly questioning whether the rate of unemployment consistent with the inflation target was higher than previously assessed, which makes 4.7% less disinflationary than it looks, and the same minutes show a committee prepared to accept slower growth and weaker employment to bring inflation down - it pre-committed to tolerating this print. The composition helps too: full-time employment rose 34,400 while part-time fell 73,700, and participation dropped to 66.80% from 67.10%. August headline CPI is 4.0% with the trimmed mean at 3.6% for a third month, so Q3 CPI on October 28, six days before the meeting, is now the whole November case.

NZD.when: October 28, a Monetary Policy Review rather than a full Statement, with centralbank.watch carrying 88% for no change; Westpac expects the pause then 3.00% in December, and TE's forecast rows agree.
NZD.note: TE re-verified the official cash rate at 2.75% after the September 2 increase from 2.50%. The new evidence runs against the currency and it comes from the bank closest to the data. ANZ's commentary of October 9 says the Selected Price Indexes confirmed some downside risk to our and the RBNZ's Q3 CPI forecasts, and Q3 CPI is the final major domestic release before the decision. That matters because the hawkish tail here was built on inflation staying above 4% - Q2 printed 4.1% against 3.1% prior and Westpac has inflation finishing 2026 above 4% - and BNZ's outlier call for an October hike and an eventual 3.75% OCR rests on the same assumption. A soft Q3 print removes the tail and leaves a currency with 5.6% unemployment, a 2.75% policy rate and the second-widest negative differential to the dollar on the board. NZD/USD at 0.56259 is plus 0.25% on the day but minus 2.28% on the month and minus 2.26% year to date.

CAD.when: October 28 with a Monetary Policy Report built on the Bank's new Prima model, then December 9; no cut is priced, and the hike odds that looked like residue a week ago now have a second consecutive week of crude behind them.
CAD.note: TE re-verified the overnight rate at 2.25%, unchanged since the September hold. The Bank's own threshold is the whole story. In Halifax on September 21 Macklem said that if oil prices stay near US$100 a barrel the Bank would expect inflation to edge up in the coming months, that it has been looking through the direct impact of higher oil so far, and that the risk of it becoming more persistent has increased; he also flagged the risk of delaying a hike too long and called the Middle East war a bigger issue for inflation than US tariffs. WTI at 94.810 is plus 7.40% on the week and within 5.5% of that number, against the Bank's own baseline assumption of crude falling toward 75 dollars by mid-2027. TD still expects a hold through 2026 while markets price at least one hike before year-end. The counterweight is domestic and severe: September employment fell 68.3K with unemployment at 6.5% and core CPI at 2.4%. Macklem speaks at 06:05 UTC today and 04:15 UTC on Friday.

CHF.when: December 10, the next quarterly assessment, with the policy meeting minutes on October 22 and Chairman Schlegel speaking tomorrow at 04:30 UTC.
CHF.note: TE re-verified the SNB policy rate at 0.00%, unchanged. There is nothing in the policy to trade and the haven test keeps failing, which is the actual finding. In a week with Houthi strikes on Riyadh's main airport, a tanker and a container ship hit in the Strait and the US Navy engaging Iranian-linked vessels, EUR/CHF rose to 0.93229 from 0.93096 and USD/CHF at 0.83186 holds a plus 4.91% year-to-date gain for the dollar. The franc lost ground to both in a week built for it. The September statement dropped the appreciation bias and Martin hinted on October 8 at lower-for-long rather than a return to negative rates, so the two-sided risk is intervention talk rather than the rate. Swiss inflation at 1.0% in September with core at 0.5% gives the Bank no reason to act in either direction before December.

strength.tag: Restored from +1 to +2 on the hawkish side of the CPI binary: core 0.3% m/m against a 0.2% consensus and core 2.6% y/y against 2.5%, with the dollar bid against six of seven majors and DXY turning to 102.448 at plus 0.26%.
strength.drivers: Fed funds upper bound 4.00% TE-verified; September CPI TE-verified on the Sep/26 rows at 3.7% y/y against a 3.6% consensus and 3.4% prior, 0.6% m/m in line, core 2.6% y/y against 2.5% and 2.4% prior, and core 0.3% m/m against a 0.2% consensus and level with a 0.3% prior - a third consecutive 0.3% core month that annualises near 3.6% on the three-month run; TE also shows energy inflation 20.40% from 16.30% and one-year consumer inflation expectations 3.90% from 3.60%; the Williams cap stands unchanged, the New York Fed President having said on October 13 that one more hike may be appropriate and that at this time he has no reason to think the Fed would need to do more after that; October 28 priced at a 22.0% hike and 78.0% hold pre-print on centralbank.watch, which had not refreshed ten minutes after the release, with December 9 across a 70-87% band; September unanimous 12-0 with all 19 officials backing it in the October 7 minutes; projection medians 4.1% for 2026 and 2027, 3.9% for 2028, 3.6% for 2029 and 3.2% longer run; September payrolls 29K after 133K; unemployment 4.2%; annual growth 2.2%; retail sales 6.0% y/y; DXY 102.448 at plus 0.26% on the day, plus 2.84% on the month and plus 3.70% year to date.
strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish into December 9 again, restored from the balanced call this file carried for a single session, and the distinction is worth keeping straight. December was never the question - Williams kept it and the committee is unanimous. What this print changes is the quality of the December case rather than its existence: a third 0.3% core month in a row is the one piece of evidence a committee cannot attribute to the Strait of Hormuz, and it arrived alongside an in-line headline, which means the oil part of September's inflation was fully priced and the surprise came from everything else. That is what reopens October 28, two weeks out, from a pre-print 22%. The far leg is where this stops, and it stops hard. The 2027 path was disowned on Tuesday by one of its own dots - a permanent voter and the most important voice on the committee after the Chair - and no September core reading reverses a statement about 2027. So the dollar is bought for a nearer and better-defended hike rather than for a higher terminal rate, which is exactly why this is plus 2 and not plus 3. The price agrees with that reading rather than a stronger one: broad but moderate, six of seven majors lower, DXY plus 0.26% rather than a break of Monday's 102.60 high. Invalidated back to plus 1 by Warsh on Friday at 03:30 UTC endorsing the Williams cap with this number in hand, or by PPI and retail sales tomorrow showing no producer-level pass-through; confirmed toward plus 3 only if October 28 reprices through 50% and the terminal-rate language is restored.

What is new is the other side of the mandate. A minus 0.1% m/m GDP print at 06:00 UTC tomorrow would be the first contraction in this cycle's run-up and the first clean reason for the six who held in September to hold again; the labour market underneath already supports them, with payrolled employees falling 26.1K and wage growth decelerating to 3.9%. Sterling is the one currency on this board where the hike has to be defended against the growth data rather than the inflation data, and the 75-90% pricing range reflects exactly that uncertainty. Four Bailey appearances this week give the committee unusual room to steer it - 05:30 UTC today, 07:30 UTC tomorrow, a red folder at 02:00 UTC Friday and 06:45 UTC Saturday. Invalidated to 0 by a GDP contraction worse than minus 0.1% combined with Bailey declining to reaffirm the energy conditional; confirmed to plus 2 by a flat or positive print that leaves November unquestioned.

strength.tag: Raised from 0 to +1 on the one leg that is hardest to fake: Lagarde moved from no evidence of energy feeding into wages to saying the Council can anticipate second-round effects, and OAT-Bund narrowed to 137.52bp from 142.98bp.

strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish into December 17 and now scored for it, with the caveat stated plainly: the policy case improved and the price did not. The language change is the whole upgrade. For a week the best argument against the December hike was Lagarde's own line that she saw no evidence at this stage of energy prices feeding into wages - an explicit statement that the Council would wait for the pass-through before acting. This morning she replaced it with a statement that the Council can anticipate rather than wait, and named wage negotiations as the signal it is watching. A central bank that acts on its forecast with HICP at 3.8% and new staff projections arriving exactly at the December meeting is a central bank that hikes, which is what 64 of 73 economists already expect. The France leg improved too and improved hawkishly: she pushed the fiscal problem back to Paris rather than hinting at support, and the spread narrowed 5.46bp anyway, through the opening of the plenary debate rather than despite it. What holds this at plus 1 is the third leg. EUR/USD is still the worst major year to date at minus 4.54% and has gained 0.10% on the week in a week when the dollar's terminal rate was capped, which is a weak response to a strong setup. The political calendar also stays live - the solemn vote on the revenue half is October 20, the social security bill October 27 and the whole text November 17, with a censure motion possible at any point and the ordinance route shut until December 17 at midnight. Invalidated to 0 by a censure motion being filed or OAT-Bund re-widening through 145bp; confirmed to plus 2 if Lagarde repeats the anticipate formulation at 08:30 UTC today and the spread holds inside 140bp.

strength.tag: Cut from +2 to +1 on its own data: September employment fell 39.3K against a plus 19.6K forecast and unemployment rose to 4.7%, tripping both of the invalidation triggers this file published yesterday, and AUD/USD at 0.69561 is the only major lower against a falling dollar.
strength.drivers: Cash rate 4.60% TE-verified after the unanimous September 29 hike from 4.35%; September employment TE-verified on the Sep/26 rows at minus 39.3K against a plus 19.6K forecast and plus 39.5K prior, with unemployment 4.7% against 4.6% expected and 4.6% prior - above the 4.6% that pre-release previews were already calling a five-year high; the composition is two-sided and TE-verified on the same page - full-time employment plus 34,400 after minus 6,300 and part-time minus 73,700 after plus 45,775, with the participation rate 66.80% from 67.10%, so the headline loss is entirely part-time and a third of a point of the labour force left rather than joined the unemployed; the September minutes still record members concerned that excess demand was greater than previously assessed, a hold considered and rejected, a readiness to raise further if required, and - the line that matters most today - the Bank's own economists increasingly questioning whether the rate of unemployment consistent with the inflation target was higher than previously assessed; August headline CPI 4.0% with the trimmed mean at 3.6% for a third month; wage growth 3.2%; annual growth 2.1%; copper 6.5672 USD/lb at minus 0.67% on the day with the year-to-date gain trimmed to 15.58% from the 18.31% carried yesterday, against iron ore 90.74 USD/T at minus 15.30% year to date; AUD/USD 0.69561 at minus 0.23% on the day against DXY minus 0.34%, EUR/USD plus 0.35%, GBP/USD plus 0.32% and NZD/USD plus 0.31%.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Balanced into November 3, down from hawkish, and the downgrade is the one this file pre-committed to: yesterday's entry said plus 2 was invalidated toward plus 1 by a print materially below plus 19.6K or unemployment above 4.6%, and both arrived in the same release. The price confirmed it in a way that leaves no ambiguity about attribution - every other major is up at least 0.31% against a dollar that is down 0.34% on DXY, and AUD is the only one lower, so this is Australian weakness rather than a dollar move. What stops it going to zero is that the RBA pre-authorised exactly this outturn. The September minutes show a committee prepared to accept slower growth and weaker employment to get inflation down, and record its own economists increasingly questioning whether the unemployment rate consistent with target is higher than previously assessed - a higher NAIRU makes 4.7% less disinflationary than the headline implies, which is the opposite of how most central banks would read it. The composition cuts the same way: full-time employment rose 34,400, the entire decline was part-time, and participation fell 0.3pp, so a meaningful share of the rise in the unemployment rate is supply leaving rather than demand collapsing. Against that, a 4.7% rate is still the first hard number to contradict the excess-demand reading the hawkish case was built on, and the terms of trade no longer help - copper's year-to-date gain has been trimmed to 15.58% from 18.31% while iron ore, the larger export, is minus 15.30%. So November is now a CPI trade and nothing else: Q3 inflation on October 28, six days before the meeting, carries the entire case. Invalidated to 0 by a Q3 trimmed mean at or below 3.4% on October 28, or by the Bank publicly reframing 4.7% as evidence demand has cooled; confirmed back toward plus 2 by a trimmed mean above 3.6% that makes the labour market the lesser of the Bank's two problems.

Two upgrades in two days needs defending, and the defence is that the leg extended rather than oscillated: WTI has gone 90.409, 92.715, 94.810 across three readings of this file, and it is now close enough to the Governor's own stated threshold that his October 28 Monetary Policy Report has to rewrite the Bank's crude assumption in public - the baseline of 75 dollars by mid-2027 is wrong by roughly 20 dollars, not marginally. That report is produced on the Bank's new Prima model, which gives it more room than usual to reframe. What caps this firmly at 0 rather than positive is a labour market that would make a hike hard to justify to anyone: minus 68.3K in September, unemployment at 6.5% and rising, the employment rate down to 60.6%, and wage growth decelerating - with core CPI at 2.4% giving the Bank no inflation cover to act on. So the trade is the removal of a short rather than the establishment of a long. Macklem speaks at 06:05 UTC today and 04:15 UTC Friday and is the fastest way this resolves. Invalidated back to minus 1 if crude retraces under 90 - the Russian diesel relief and the sharp September OPEC+ output gain are live bearish legs - and confirmed to plus 1 only if WTI holds above 95 into the Monetary Policy Report and Macklem drops the looking-through language.

strength.tag: Unchanged at 0 on arithmetic rather than policy: the ten-year gap widened to 220.60bp from 219.40bp because JGBs rallied alongside Treasuries, so the firmest December pricing the yen has carried still buys it nothing.
strength.drivers: Policy rate 1.25% TE-verified after the September 18 hike from 1.00%; October 29-30 confirmed from boj.or.jp with the Outlook Report on October 30 and December 17-18 the next meeting with no Outlook Report; October priced as a hold at 91-94% on prediction markets and 91% on centralbank.watch as of October 9, while swaps imply roughly 90% for a hike by December; US ten-year 5.2070% against the JGB at 3.0010% is 220.60bp, wider than the 219.40bp carried yesterday; August CPI 1.9% with core at 1.7% from 1.8%; unemployment 2.5% with unemployed persons up to 1.77 million; wage growth 3.8% after 4.3%; annual growth 0.7% after 0.5%; retail sales 2.7% y/y; USD/JPY 158.159 at minus 0.11% on the day and plus 0.05% on the week, back below the 158.50 area where intervention commentary starts, and still plus 1.97% on the month; Japan reported to have intervened in late July with US participation, with future dollar-selling to be financed through the Fed's FIMA repo facility.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Balanced into October 30, and the reason a 90% December is still not enough is worth stating precisely. The yen does not need the BoJ to hike; it needs the gap to compress. Last night offered the ideal setup for that - the Fed's terminal rate was capped by its most important non-Chair voice - and the gap widened anyway, to 220.60bp from 219.40bp, because JGBs rallied in sympathy with Treasuries rather than standing still. A Fed that still delivers December while the BoJ is 90% to move in the same month leaves the expected differential unchanged, and the spot differential got worse. That is the whole case for staying at 0 rather than upgrading on the Williams headline. Two things could change it. The first is the Outlook Report on October 30, which is where a revised path actually gets published and where the under-priced structural story - a government that has stopped treating deflation as the binding constraint - would show up; note December has no Outlook Report, so October 30 is the last scheduled chance this year. The second is the Ministry of Finance: 158.50 is where the commentary starts, and the July operation with US participation and FIMA financing means the threat is not rhetorical. Invalidated to plus 1 if the gap compresses through 215bp or the Outlook Report lifts the inflation path; invalidated to minus 1 if a soft core CPI today pushes US yields down while the BoJ signals a December pause.

strength.tag: Unchanged at 0 and the negative finding replicated again: in a week with strikes on Riyadh's main airport and two more vessels hit in the Strait, EUR/CHF rose to 0.93229 from 0.93096 and the franc lost ground to both reference currencies.

This week ran the haven test at maximum intensity - Houthi strikes on Riyadh's main airport, Trump saying the US may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, a tanker and a container ship struck in the Strait on Tuesday per UKMTO notices, the US Navy engaging Iranian-linked vessels - and the franc fell against the euro and gave back only a fraction against the dollar, which still holds a 4.91% year-to-date gain on it. So the franc crosses are traded on the other leg rather than on the next headline, and the clearest expression of that today is EUR/CHF long now that the ECB has turned pre-emptive while the SNB has nothing scheduled before December 10. Policy will not supply a surprise: inflation at 1.0% with core at 0.5% and unemployment at 3.0% leaves the Bank no reason to move in either direction, and the September statement already dropped the appreciation bias. ANZ, reading the Selected Price Indexes that feed the quarterly print, says they confirmed some downside risk to its own and to the RBNZ's Q3 CPI forecasts. If the Q3 print lands soft, what remains is the weakest fundamental set on this board: 5.6% unemployment, the highest here, a 2.75% policy rate that is the second lowest, wage growth of 2.1% that is the slowest, and a negative differential to the dollar that a 2.6% growth rate does not offset. The October 28 meeting being a Review rather than a Statement limits how much the Bank can reframe it either way. The right expression is in the crosses rather than against the dollar, because the dollar leg is the one that just got capped - AUD/NZD and GBP/NZD carry the policy divergence without the CPI binary at 12:30 UTC today. catalysts.event: US: New York Fed President Williams rules out a 2027 hike (Bloomberg interview)
catalysts.note: The largest piece of new evidence on the board and the reason the dollar was cut to plus 1. Williams said he has not changed his view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike and that at this time he has no reason to think the Fed would need to do more after that, adding that it's still mid-October and the data will decide. That keeps December but caps the terminal rate, and it directly contradicts the September projection table's 2027 dots - 8 of 18 participants at 4.375% and 14 of 18 at or above the 4.1% median - of which Williams is one. The dollar fell against all seven majors on the session and the ten-year eased about 3bp to 5.2070.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB President Lagarde speaks in Bangkok (IMF sidelines, first of two today)
catalysts.note: She changed the operative sentence. Euro-area inflation is driven predominantly, but not exclusively, by higher energy prices linked to the Iran war; the Council has not yet seen second-round effects in broader prices but is watching early signals, especially in wage negotiations; and we cannot wait until they're there in full view, but we can anticipate. That replaces the line this file has quoted for a week, that she saw no evidence at this stage of energy feeding into wages, and it is why the euro was raised to plus 1. On France she said some countries face disproportionate borrowing costs, with France being a case in point, but that the primary and first solution lies at home in France and it has to do with fiscal policies; she did not rule out the Transmission Protection Instrument.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: The first of four Bailey appearances this week. The line the market is testing is his own conditional - that higher energy costs have had a limited effect on wages and prices so far, but the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate - against UK gas up 11.04% on the week and 191.29% year to date. November 5 is priced across a 75-90% range rather than as a certainty, so each appearance can move it.

catalysts.note: The fastest way the Canadian upgrade to 0 resolves. catalysts.event: US: September CPI - headline, core, m/m and y/y (ForexFactory red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered the hawkish side of the binary. All four lines are TE-verified on the Sep/26 rows: core CPI 0.3% m/m against a 0.2% consensus and level with the 0.3% prior, core 2.6% y/y against 2.5% and up from 2.4%, headline 3.7% y/y against 3.6% and up from 3.4%, and headline 0.6% m/m exactly in line. The in-line headline is the tell - September's energy spike was fully priced, so the surprise came from the part that is not oil, with TE also showing energy inflation at 20.40% from 16.30% and one-year consumer inflation expectations at 3.90% from 3.60%. A third consecutive 0.3% core month annualises near 3.6% on the three-month run, against the 2.4% core y/y the Fed cited in September. The dollar was restored to plus 2, DXY turned to 102.448 at plus 0.26%, and October 28 is live again from a pre-print 22.0%. The Williams cap on 2027 is untouched by it.

catalysts.note: Forecast minus 0.1% against plus 0.4% prior. A contraction is the first clean argument for the six MPC members who held in September to hold again, and it is the reason sterling's risk has rotated from the inflation side to the growth side. The labour market underneath already supports them, with payrolled employees minus 26.1K and wage growth decelerating to 3.9% from 4.2%.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: Ninety minutes after the GDP print, which makes this the most informative of his four appearances this week. Whether he reaffirms the energy conditional after a contraction is the clearest read available on whether November 5 stays in the 75-90% band.

catalysts.event: Euro area: EU Economic Summit (day two)
catalysts.note: Second day. Same relevance as day one: fiscal and energy headlines while the French budget is in plenary debate.

catalysts.event: US: September PPI and retail sales (ForexFactory red folder)
catalysts.note: PPI m/m forecast 0.6% against 0.4% prior and core PPI 0.3% against 0.2%; retail sales m/m 0.3% against 1.2% and core retail sales 0.6% against 1.4%. The second half of the inflation test and the first read on whether the energy shock is being passed through at the producer level. Retail sales also matter to the growth side, with the prior month's 1.2% a difficult comparison and annual retail sales running at 6.0%.

catalysts.event: US: Philly Fed manufacturing index and weekly jobless claims
catalysts.note: Philly Fed forecast 28.2 against 37.8 prior and claims 199K against 197K. Claims near 200K remain inconsistent with September payrolls of 29K, and that gap is the main unresolved question in the US labour data.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks (ForexFactory red folder)
catalysts.note: His third appearance of the week and the one ForexFactory flags as high impact, landing after both the GDP print and his Thursday remarks. The November 5 meeting carries a Monetary Policy Report and the committee is 6-3, so any shift in how he frames the energy conditional moves the 75-90% pricing directly.

catalysts.event: US: Fed Chairman Warsh speaks (ForexFactory red folder)
catalysts.note: The only voice that outranks the one that moved the market on Tuesday. Williams capped the 2027 path; whether the Chair endorses, ignores or contradicts that is the single most consequential thing scheduled this week after CPI. It lands two days after the inflation print, so he will be speaking with the number in hand.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC Governor Macklem speaks
catalysts.note: His second appearance of the week, twelve days before the October 28 Monetary Policy Report that has to rewrite the Bank's crude assumption in public.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: Fourth and final appearance of the week.

catalysts.event: France: National Assembly solemn vote on the revenue half of the 2027 budget
catalysts.note: The first hard date in the budget timetable and the first realistic window for a censure motion, though one can be filed at any point in the debate. The social security bill follows on October 27 and the whole text on November 17; the ordinance route is unavailable until the 70-day period expires on December 17 at midnight. Lecornu brings roughly 54bn euros of consolidation to an Assembly where he has no majority. OAT-Bund narrowed to 137.52bp on October 13 closes from 142.98bp, so the market is currently pricing survival.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB policy meeting minutes
catalysts.note: The record of the September assessment that left the policy rate at 0.00% and dropped the appreciation bias. Watch for how much weight the Bank gave the energy shock and whether intervention was discussed.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 CPI (expected week of October 19-26)
catalysts.note: The final major domestic release before the October 28 decision and the number that decides whether the kiwi stays at minus 1 or falls to minus 2. ANZ's commentary of October 9 says the Selected Price Indexes confirmed some downside risk to its own and the RBNZ's Q3 forecasts. Q2 printed 4.1% against 3.1% prior; a soft Q3 removes the hawkish tail that BNZ's outlier call for a 3.75% OCR rests on.

catalysts.event: US: FOMC decision (no projections)
catalysts.note: Reopened by the September CPI print, which is precisely the reading this file named as what would reopen it. Pre-print pricing was a hold at 78.0% and a hike at 22.0% on centralbank.watch, and that screen still read the same within ten minutes of the release, so the post-print probability is not yet verifiable. There are no projections at this meeting, and Warsh speaks on Friday with the number in hand.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report (new Prima model)
catalysts.note: The report where the Bank's crude assumption - still a baseline of oil falling toward 75 dollars by mid-2027 - gets rewritten against a WTI of 94.810. TD expects a hold through 2026 while markets price at least one hike before year-end. The first Monetary Policy Report produced on the Bank's new Prima model, which gives it more room than usual to reframe.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review
catalysts.note: A Review rather than a full Monetary Policy Statement, which limits how much the Bank can reframe. Priced 88% for no change at 2.75%; Westpac expects the pause then 3.00% on December 9, matching TE's forecast rows.

catalysts.event: Australia: Q3 CPI
catalysts.note: Six days before the November 3 RBA meeting and the number that actually decides it. The trimmed mean the Bank weighs has been 3.6% for three months against August headline of 4.0%. ANZ has November more likely than not, Westpac carries 4.85% by December, CBA sees a higher bar.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB decision (no projections)
catalysts.note: Expected to hold the deposit rate at 2.50% by 70 of 73 economists in the Reuters poll of October 5-8. The hike is December 17, when new staff projections arrive, and 64 of the same 73 expect it. After this morning's anticipate formulation, the press conference is where the pre-emptive framing either hardens or softens.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ decision and Outlook Report
catalysts.note: October 29-30 confirmed from boj.or.jp. The decision is settled as a hold at 91-94%, but the Outlook Report is the asymmetric part and it is the last one scheduled this year - the December 17-18 meeting carries none. Swaps imply roughly 90% for a hike by December, so this is where the path gets published rather than where the move happens.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA decision
catalysts.note: Live on the September minutes, which record members concerned that excess demand was greater than previously assessed and ready to act including increasing the cash rate target further if required. Decided by the October 28 Q3 CPI.

catalysts.event: UK: BoE decision and Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.note: Priced across a 75-90% range depending on source rather than as a near-certainty, with the committee at 6-3 after September. The growth data is now the obstacle: GDP m/m tomorrow is forecast at minus 0.1%.

catalysts.event: US: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.note: Priced 83.0% for that date and 86.7% cumulatively on centralbank.watch, near 75% on wire trackers and near 70% on CME-derived readings. The more interesting part is now the projection table rather than the decision: Williams has said in public he sees no need for a 2027 hike, and the September dots have 14 of 18 participants at or above a 4.1% median for 2027. December is where that contradiction gets resolved on paper.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB quarterly policy assessment
catalysts.note: The next scheduled chance for the SNB to do anything, from a policy rate of 0.00% with inflation at 1.0% and core at 0.5%.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB decision with new staff projections
catalysts.note: The meeting 64 of 73 economists expect to deliver 25bp to a 2.75% deposit rate. Also the midnight deadline after which the French government's ordinance route on the 2027 budget becomes available.

catalysts.event: Iran / Strait of Hormuz / Saudi-Houthi escalation
catalysts.note: The regime driver for crude, the Canadian dollar, the two equity indices and the failed franc haven bid. Two-sided for the first time in two weeks - see the geopolitics note.

catalysts.event: Russian diesel sanctions relief and OPEC+ September output
catalysts.note: The new bearish leg in crude. Trump said Russia would supply diesel to global markets and his administration temporarily eased sanctions on Russian fuel; OPEC reported a sharp September production gain led by Saudi Arabia; Saudi Arabia said its exports are not at risk. Goldman's check: an extra 800,000 tonnes cuts wholesale diesel by only one to two dollars a barrel on the US Gulf Coast and in Europe, against US inventories down 14% year on year and visible Chinese stocks down 11%.

catalysts.event: Japan Ministry of Finance intervention risk below 158.50
catalysts.note: USD/JPY at 158.159 sits in the zone where commentary starts. Japan is reported to have intervened in late July with US participation, and the finance ministry has said future dollar-selling intervention would be financed through the Fed's FIMA repo facility, which is an unusual arrangement and the reason the threat is not rhetorical.

geopolitics: The oil story became genuinely two-sided this week for the first time since the Hormuz escalation began, and the cleanest evidence is that the two crude benchmarks split on Tuesday: Brent settled 105.69, down 96 cents, while WTI settled 94.14, up 40 cents. This morning both are higher again on TE - WTI 94.810 at plus 0.71% on the day and plus 7.40% on the week, Brent 106.338 at plus 0.61% and plus 6.13% - but the spread between them has compressed to roughly 11.5 dollars, and that compression is the market re-sorting which barrels are actually at risk. On the bullish side nothing has improved. Houthi strikes hit Riyadh's main airport, Trump said the US may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis and separately suggested Iran may be behind the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in order to push oil prices up, a tanker and a container ship were struck in the Strait on Tuesday according to UK Maritime Trade Operations notices, Iranian state media claimed a tanker attempting an unauthorised crossing caught fire, and CENTCOM said US forces helped partners move more than 19 million barrels through the Strait on Monday - a figure a command only publicises when transit itself is the problem. Kpler counted ten tankers struck in the Strait between September 28 and October 4, a record. On the bearish side, three things arrived at once and they are new. Trump said Russia would supply diesel to global markets and his administration temporarily eased sanctions on Russian fuel; Saudi Arabia stated publicly that its exports are not at risk; and OPEC reported that OPEC+ production posted a sharp gain in September, driven by an increase from Saudi Arabia. Goldman supplied the arithmetic that keeps this in proportion: an extra 800,000 metric tonnes of diesel would cut wholesale prices on the US Gulf Coast and in Europe by only one to two dollars a barrel, against US inventories down 14% year on year and visible Chinese stocks down 11%. So the relief is real but small relative to the risk, which is why the bias here stays long crude while the conviction stays LOW-MED and the monthly chart stays down 10.41%. The FX transmission is where the interesting change is. For three sessions this board ran on a simple chain: crude up, US inflation expectations up, December Fed hike odds up, dollar up. That chain broke overnight. Crude extended another 7.40% on the week and the dollar fell against all seven majors, because Williams capped the Fed's terminal rate and a supply shock is exactly the kind of inflation a committee can choose to look through - Lagarde made the same point from the other side of the Atlantic this morning, describing euro-area inflation as driven predominantly by energy linked to the Iran war while saying the Council has not yet seen second-round effects. What survives the break is the direct transmission rather than the monetary one. Canada is the clearest case: WTI at 94.810 is within 5.5% of the hundred dollars Macklem named in Halifax as the level at which the Bank would expect inflation to edge up rather than look through, against a published baseline of crude falling toward 75 dollars by mid-2027, and that is why Canada was raised to 0 today. The European gas leg is the second: EU gas at 86.76 EUR/MWh is plus 11.12% on the week and plus 208.09% year to date, German gas at 88.16 is plus 14.99% on the week, UK gas at 215.00 GBp/thm is plus 11.04% on the week and plus 191.29% year to date - which is the direct input into Bailey's conditional that the longer this volatility persists, the more likely it is the Bank will need to raise Bank Rate, and a headwind for the GER40 short. The third and most instructive is the franc, which did nothing. Through a week of strikes on Riyadh's main airport, two more vessels hit in the Strait and the US Navy engaging Iranian-linked vessels, EUR/CHF rose to 0.93229 from 0.93096 and the dollar held a 4.91% year-to-date gain against it. The haven premium is being competed away by yield, because the franc pays 0.00% while every other central bank on this board is hiking or has just hiked. Gold makes the same point at scale: 4165.35 is minus 3.58% year to date in a year with a war, a disrupted Strait and crude up 65.12%, because its axis is US real rates and those rose all year. That is why the correct response to the next escalation headline is to trade the currency with the direct energy exposure - CAD, and the European gas-sensitive crosses - rather than to buy the traditional havens, which have now failed the test repeatedly and in public.
